stories.headline: Brisbane Lions produce stuff of football immortality to claim three-peat
stories.summary: The Brisbane Lions etched their name into football folklore winning a third successive premiership, and their stunning Grand Final victory may never be bettered for drama or resilience, writes Rohan Connolly.
stories.body:
There's barely enough superlatives to describe a team good enough to win three premierships in a row. But what about one which not only achieves a three-peat, but does it the hard way three years straight, and just for good measure pulls off the most insane comeback in Grand Final history in the third and final leg?

That's the stuff of football immortality. And that's where Brisbane stands right now, having become only the second club in VFL/AFL history to win a second flag hat trick, following Melbourne in the mid-1950s.

The Demons, though, were dominant right through their second three-flag run between 1955-57. Brisbane has had to pull rabbit after rabbit out of the hat, in 2024 coming from fifth to victory, and last year bouncing back from a qualifying-final belting.

And now, this. Just three weeks ago, the Lions were absolutely smashed by Sydney to the tune of 53 points in a qualifying-final defeat which might have destroyed a team made of lesser stuff.

But what happened subsequently may never be bettered for drama or resilience in the midst of a finals campaign.

First, the Lions recovered their composure quickly enough to put Adelaide to the sword in a semifinal. Last week, they survived a withering Hawthorn comeback, trailing with little more than a minute left when Hugh McCluggage's tackle on Jarman Impey got them over the line.

That would have been more than enough September heroics to make this premiership very special regardless of what happened on Grand Final day. But now we have a win in the most important game of all which will be very hard to top.

A good 45 minutes after the final siren, it was still almost impossible to believe. With only four minutes 18 seconds left to play, Brisbane trailed by 17 points.

Remember that the biggest margin overhauled at three-quarter time of a Grand Final is only 23 points, in 1984. And Essendon had that deficit erased within eight minutes. How Brisbane conjured this Houdini trick is already the stuff of football legend.

Make no mistake. While Carlton's famous comeback from 44 points down at halftime of the 1970 Grand Final against Collingwood remains the gold standard of premiership-deciding revivals, this one, given the lateness of the hour, doesn't pale much in comparison.

The incredible Lions peeled off the last four goals of the game in just 250 seconds. The first, from Charlie Cameron didn't even provoke that much excitement from most of the 100,023 assembled, such was the feeling Fremantle was about to break its premiership duck.

That changed dramatically, however, when Zac Bailey snapped an amazing goal from a thicket of congestion with only another 24 seconds of play having elapsed. And then came Logan Morris.

Brisbane is replete with players who can have done very little throughout the course of a game and still win it. This week, it was the 21-year-old's turn.

Morris had had just eight disposals for 1.1 when, with 90-odd seconds left, he took the single most important mark of the game, a strong contested grab in front of Oscar McDonald. From 45 metres and with ice flowing through his veins, Morris put the Lions in front for the last time.

If that wasn't enough, he made sure of this famous win with a beautiful curling right foot snap from 35 metres. Seven points the difference now, just eight seconds left and game, set and match.

They just don't know how to quit, these Lions. They didn't when they overhauled a seven-goal deficit in a 2024 semifinal on their way to the first leg of this three-peat. They climbed off the canvas again that year's preliminary final.

Last week, they appeared to have blown another preliminary final until conjuring two goals in the last minute. And now a trick to top perhaps anything we've seen on the Grand Final stage.

"We probably thought it was starting to slip away, no doubt about it," Brisbane co-captain Hugh McCluggage told ESPN in the jubilant Lions' rooms after the game. "But we saw last week, this group just finds a way when it gets tough, and in a way it just felt like it was meant to be today after last week."

The sounding of "Wharfie Time" after Patrick Voss appeared to have clinched the premiership for the Dockers might have been a red rag to a bull for the Lions, but McCluggage said the incredible resolve goes back a lot further than that.

"We've done a lot of work over 10 years building our connection, building our brotherhood for moments like that," he said. "And it's a lot of butcher's paper sessions in the offseason, and days toiling down at Coorparoo in the heat, and it all pays off on days like this."

Coach Chris Fagan, sitting among the three premiership cups now literally with his fingerprints all over them, mirrored McCluggage's doubts with less than four-and-a-half minutes left on the clock.

"I thought we were in a little bit of trouble," he told ESPN with characteristic understatement. "The rate at which we were scoring during the game, it didn't look like it was going to happen. But, you know, we've got our strategies in place where if we've got to win the game, we'll roll the dice a little bit and try a few things. We're fortunate that we got the ball out in the middle, which is something we didn't really do all day.

"I just think over time we've just developed a great belief in ourselves. I feel like we're never out of it. So today was sort of like when it all came together, I suppose."

To say that sounded like someone reflecting on the culmination of a long-term project come to a successful conclusion might be an overstatement, but if Fagan does decide to pull the pin on the coaching caper, would any many man ever have gone out more on top than he?

"Oh well, I've been doing it for 10 years," he said. "It takes a lot out of you. I haven't made up my mind yet, but I sort of always had this idea that it would be good to walk away when you're on top rather than walking away when you're going no good at all."

No chance of that now. And what of the team he'd be leaving behind? They'll be in good hands whoever happened to take the reins. Because that coach will know first and foremost that not only is he in charge of the most talented and successful list in the AFL, he'll also be at the helm of a group that just doesn't know how to give up.

You can read more of Rohan Connolly's work at FOOTYOLOGY.

stories.headline: Man City verdict will leave a stain and stench on a Premier League era
stories.summary: Manchester City are expected to be found guilty of almost all 115 financial charges against them. It means an era of English soccer is now tarnished with multiple asterisks.
stories.body:
It was one of the Premier League's most iconic moments: May 2014 and Steven Gerrard, Liverpool's heroic captain, finally lifts the Premier League trophy alongside manager Brendan Rodgers, who ended the club's quarter-century wait to become champions of England once again. What a story.

England's fallen giants were back on their perch, and Gerrard, the greatest player never to win a title medal, was able to put the seal on a glorious career with the one major honor missing from his collection. Except it didn't happen. Just like Jose Mourinho winning his fourth Premier League title with Manchester United didn't happen four years later.

Perhaps in a parallel universe Liverpool are listed as 2013-14 Premier League champions and United in 2017-18, but in the real world, Manchester City came out on top on both occasions and on many more. But did they really?

The news that City are expected to be found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges related to breaching Premier League financial regulations between 2009 and 2018 -- neither City nor the Premier League deny the verdict of the independent panel -- means that everything they achieved during that period is now in question. City have consistently denied all the charges and are expected to appeal the verdict.

Forget the asterisks next to those title wins and cup triumphs -- those moments that have been imprinted forever on the fabric of English football. The imprints are still there -- they will never go away -- but neither will the stain and the stench of being found guilty of breaking the rules -- cheating -- to claim their own glorious moments and, just as importantly, deny others from experiencing them.

So next time you see a replay of Sergio Aguero's famous title-winning goal in the final seconds of the 3-2 win against Queen's Park Rangers on the final day of the 2011-12 season, ask yourself whether it is valid. Or more likely, the footage becomes nothing more than the Premier League's version of Ben Johnson sprinting to gold in the 1988 Olympics 100-meter final or any of the seven consecutive Tour de France wins by Lance Armstrong between 1999 and 2005.

Johnson and Armstrong were both unmasked as drug cheats and stripped of their titles. That may yet happen to City when the Premier League rolls out its sanctions for the industrial scale breaches that the club has been found guilty of -- massive fines and points deductions which could lead to relegation are likely -- but the problem is that nobody really remembers who came second in an unfair race.

Who did Armstrong beat into second place in those seven successive wins? Good luck answering that without using Wikipedia. But for those like Gerrard, Rodgers and Mourinho, finishing second to City had its costs and real-life consequences.

Gerrard would retire without ever having won the Premier League, and he has since admitted that his slip in a 2-0 home defeat against Chelsea, which tilted the title race in City's favour, still haunts him every day. Mourinho was fired by United months after finishing second to City in 2018 -- a feat he described at the time as his "greatest achievement" due to the power of his opponent -- while Rodgers never recovered from Liverpool's failure to win the title and was gone from Anfield just over a year later.

Former United defender Rio Ferdinand, part of the team that missed out on the title by goal difference to City in 2012, reacted to news of the 114 charges by saying, "Another Premier League medal to be added to the cabinet," while former teammate David de Gea, who finished second in 2012 and 2018, posted on X, "So...Let's talk. How many Premier League titles have I won then?"

But it goes deeper than clubs, players and managers who narrowly missed out in second place because City spent beyond their means, paying higher wages and transfer fees because of inflated sponsorship deals and off-the-books payments.

Arsenal arguably took a decade to recover from having their squad repeatedly raided by City in the early years of Abu Dhabi ownership, while United have never been the same powerhouse since Carlos Tevez left Old Trafford for City in the summer of 2009, sparking the club's rise to dominance.

Former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger once used the phrase "financial doping" to describe Chelsea's lavish spending under Russian owner Roman Abramovich -- Mourinho benefited more than most with those millions building his back-to-back title-winning team at Stamford Bridge -- but City took it to a different level.

Arsenal were victims of the early spending spree at City, described at the time by then-CEO Garry Cook as the club's "accelerated acquisition strategy," with a succession of players being lured away from the Emirates for huge fees and salaries.

Kolo Toure, Emmanuel Adebayor, Bacary Sagna, Gael Clichy and Samir Nasri all made the move from Arsenal to City during the 2009-2018 period investigated by the Premier League.

Arsenal needed the money after borrowing funds to build the Emirates, but City -- a team that had not won a trophy since 1976 and had been in the third tier as recently as 1999 -- suddenly became a dream destination for players and, bankrolled by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al Nahyan, they ruthlessly raided Wenger's team time and again to build their own empire and diminish Arsenal's.

Arsenal have since recovered, becoming champions again last season under manager Mikel Arteta, who once worked as an assistant coach to Guardiola at City. However, even though the period between 2018 and the present day is not covered by the Premier League investigation, the power and prestige gained by City during that period -- they are the only English club with an unbroken Champions League qualification record since first playing in the competition in 2011 -- made them such a formidable rival for Arteta's team to overcome.

Would Guardiola, Erling Haaland, Rodri, Kevin De Bruyne, Aguero and so many more star names have chosen City over other clubs without the rule-breaking that allowed them to become the most successful team in the country? In a sport where money rules, the answer is an easy one to find.

Money has ruled, and City have prospered, but when the expected guilty verdict is made, their achievements will officially have been made by breaking the rules. The price on their ticket will now be a very heavy one.

It could mean a massive points deduction that could lead to relegation, huge fines that could financially ruin the club, sponsors deserting due to reputational damage, players wanting to leave, and those who don't might have to go anyway, their salaries no longer affordable.

City are likely to face legal action from rival clubs for loss of earnings, titles, European qualification and commercial revenue; the ramifications are endless. In 2024, Arsenal, Liverpool, United and Tottenham served legal notices on City, reserving the right to seek compensation if the club were found guilty of serious charges.

City's Abu Dhabi hierarchy may also be driven out of the game for overseeing the prolonged rule-breaking, which makes them unfit for office. If buying City in 2008 really was an Abu Dhabi sportswashing project, designed to polish the Gulf state's global brand, the end result was incalculable damage.

Yet even if Gerrard, Rodgers, Mourinho, Ferdinand, De Gea and the rest suddenly wake up one morning to the delivery of an overdue winners' medal, it won't make up for what happened at the time.

But if you never see Aguero's title-winning goal replayed on TV again, you now know why.

stories.headline: Updated: NRL 2026 team-by-team season review
stories.summary: The 2026 NRL season proper has come to an end, so it's time to evaluate every team's year.
stories.body:
The 2026 NRL season proper has come to an end, so it's time to evaluate every team's year. We take a look back at our preseason prediction, assess the way each team travelled, and work out their grades for 2026.

This will be updated as every team's season finishes.

Brisbane Broncos
Last year's ladder finish: 4th (Premiers)

Predicted 2026 finish: 3rd

Actual finish: 14th

Grade: F

Very rarely does a premiership winning side fall so far, so quickly. Everyone fully expected that the Broncos would mount an impressive title defence on the back of what they achieved in 2025 and the relative stability of their squad. What the pundits and fans could not predict was the behind-the-scenes discourse, the injuries to key players, and the apparent complete lack of commitment from players out in the middle. The coach losing the locker room is an often-used excuse, usually followed by the sacking of the coach, but Michael Maguire was only in his second season at the club after bringing them premiership glory in his first year. The players have to be held accountable for this unsightly collapse.

Where to from here: Adam Reynolds has retired, Payne Haas is off to the Rabbitohs, and the talk is that the players are not happy with coach Maguire. Mitch Barnett is coming to replace Haas, Dane Gagai to shore up the backline, and Jonah Pezet to reset the halves. They have the entire offseason to sort themselves out, a similar season in 2027 would be completely intolerable for the proud club.

Canberra Raiders
Last year's ladder finish: 1st

Predicted 2026 finish: 7th

Actual finish: 11th

Grade: D

The Raiders took out the minor premiership last season, but the way they crashed out of the finals was not encouraging when it came to predicting their 2026 run. They still should have played finals football this year and, as they showed against the Cowboys in the final round, they still have all the weapons to challenge the top sides. Hudson Young's injury certainly didn't help as they battled for a spot in the Top 8, nor did their ability to lose games they had seemingly already won.

Where to from here: They have lost several players ahead of next season, without making any moves on the player market. They will rely on the juniors coming through as well as halfback Coby Black, who lived up to all the hype during his debut performance against the Cowboys in the final round.

Canterbury Bankstown Bulldogs
Last year's ladder finish: 3rd

Predicted 2026 finish: 2nd

Actual finish: 12th

Grade: F

The Bulldogs receive an F for their 2026 season, simply because they were expected to build on their 2025 success, not crumble in the opposite direction. Lachlan Galvin proved that he is a star of the near future and probably the club's best player through the year, but he played halfback when the team needed a genuine halfback. Moving Matt Burton to centre saw him improve with new found freedom out wide, but moving Stephen Crichton to five-eighth hamstrung his best assets. The whole team continued to look completely lost in attack and only finished as high as they did through defensive resolve, which also faded at the back end of the season. Such a disappointing effort.

Where to from here: Freddy Lussick arrives to hopefully fix one part of the spine. Either Mitchell Woods or Alex Conti should be ready to pull on the No. 7 jersey, Galvin will rise to star status wider of the ruck in the No. 6 jersey, and Burton and Crichton can form the most expensive and lethal of centre combinations. All the club needs then is an attack coach, a dangerous fullback, a new lock and some more grunt in the front row. Easy!

Cronulla Sharks
Last year's ladder finish: 5th

Predicted 2026 finish: 10th

Actual finish: 5th

Grade: C

The Sharks receive a C because they were expected to take a tumble down the ladder after another disappointing finals series last year, but rallied through the season to finish fifth. There were times when they looked certain to finish in the Top 4, but lost their way near the end when Braydon Trindall was injured. They struggled with consistency, looking like world beaters for chunks of the season, but totally lost at other times. Addin Fonua-Blake once again proved his worth to the team, but could have used a bit of help. Nicho Hynes and Trindall worked really well together in the halves and Blayke Brailey was always sharp out of dummy-half. If anything their outside backs started to look a little tired and in need of a freshen up. They limped into the finals in the middle of a slump from which they never really recovered.

Where to from here: The Sharks are putting a broom through the roster, without making any major recruitment moves. Gone are Sione Katoa, Mawene Hiroti, Cameron McInnes, Jesse Ramien and Siosifa Talakai, with a couple of Super League imports their main gains. They will rely on their pathways to develop the young talent needed to build their 2027 starting team. The glory days of 2016 drift further into the past with each disappointing season.

Dolphins
Last year's ladder finish: 9th

Predicted 2026 finish: 6th

Actual finish: 3rd

Grade: B+

The Dolphins have been threatening to play finals football since entering the NRL, and they finally made the jump in the second year of Kristian Woolf's coaching tenure. It has been what can only be considered an outstanding season for the Dolphins, despite the disappointing finish against the Roosters. Having assembled one of the league's best backlines, the Dolphins were never really out of any game during the year, enabling them to survive a nasty habit of starting games slowly. They appear to be one or two key forwards short of being unstoppable and should return to finals football next season and for many years to come.

Where to from here: Coach Kristian Woolf will have to squeeze a little bit extra out of the current roster, as they have not made any acquisitions as yet. They do say goodbye to some big-name players in Jake Averillo, Jamayne Isaako, Oryn Keeley, Kodi Nikorima, Daniel Saifiti, and Ray Stone. They will look to the youngsters coming through the grades, with their Queensland Cup side showing plenty of promise having just won its Grand Final.

Gold Coast Titans
Last year's ladder finish: 16th

Predicted 2026 finish: 14th

Actual finish: 16th

Grade: D

We predicted the Titans would improve slightly under coach Josh Hannay, but they stayed in exactly the same spot. It must be so frustrating for everyone involved to watch the patches of sensational football this club is capable of playing at times. Jayden Campbell remains an elite attacking weapon, Keano Kini an amazing young talent at fullback, Cooper Bai an explosive forward and Tino Fa'asuamaleaui a stoic leader. But, they just lack a couple of key pieces and the drive to play a full 80 minutes of totally committed football.

Where to from here: Apart from welcoming Sharks centre Mawene Hiroti in 2027 they haven't made too many moves on the player market and will be looking instead to improve their systems and fitness. Hannay has a long road ahead of him, with the Bears joining the fray next season, the Titans will face another rung on that ladder they failed to climb at all in 2026.

Manly Sea Eagles
Last year's ladder finish: 10th

Predicted 2026 finish: 13th

Actual finish: 9th

Grade: C

The Sea Eagles started the season where they left off in 2025, losing and looking like a team headed down the ladder. They sacked Anthony Seibold and hired club legend Kieran Foran as head coach and went on an incredible run, which looked certain to take them into the finals. They lost Tom Trbojevic to injury and managed to keep going, but subsequently losing Luke Brooks brought the winning run to a grinding halt. Overall it was a very mixed year, which ended in a frustrating ninth place finish.

Where to from here: They lose Reuben Garrick to the Roosters next year and have made some minor acquisitions. Foran will have a full offseason with the side and they have some promising talent coming through at the club including halfback Joey Walsh. It will be interesting to see whether Foran can recapture the magic of his early days in the job, as they battle again to play finals football.

Melbourne Storm
Last year's ladder finish: 2nd (Runners-up)

Predicted 2026 finish: 8th

Actual finish: 10th

Grade: D

We tipped the Storm to take a slide down the ladder after losing last year's grand final to the Broncos, but no one ever really expects them to miss the finals. They did have a horror year with injuries, with their superstar spine seldom complete for any number of consecutive games. When they did have Harry Grant, Jahrome Hughes and Cameron Munster they were capable of beating anyone, but the bit-part players were unable to lift in their absence. Injuries aside, the Storm didn't look like the Storm at times, with defensive lapses and handling errors driving coach Craig Bellamy up the wall.

Where to from here: Bellamy is going around again as coach, which is handy as it would have been an injustice for him to leave the Storm after that season. They are revamping their backline with the addition of Dolphins flyer Jamayne Isaako and Bulldogs centre Bronson Xerri, while adding Eels forward Kelma Tuilagi. They are also losing a raft of players including Tyran Wishart and Nick Meaney, both to the Bears.

Newcastle Knights
Last year's ladder finish: 17th

Predicted 2026 finish: 13th

Actual finish: 7th

Grade: TBD

Where to from here: TBD

New Zealand Warriors
Last year's ladder finish: 6th

Predicted 2025 finish: 9th

Actual finish: 2nd

Grade: B-

Considering we expected the Warriors to miss the finals, for them to be challenging the Panthers for the minor premiership right until the final round makes this a successful season and worthy of a B. The way they crashed out of the finals in straight sets, very nearly drops them back to a C. How disappointing for Warriors fans everywhere to see them fall to the Dolphins and Knights in front of adoring home crowds. Their efforts against the Knights in front of a packed Eden Park will haunt them for many years to come. They had trouble all season keeping a starting pair of halves fit, but managed to finish second on the ladder with Chanel Harris-Tavita and Te Maire Martin working well together. Their pack, led by James Fisher-Harris, was one of the most destructive in the league, but they just weren't able to put it all together in the big games, when it really mattered.

Where to from here: The Warriors lose a raft of players, led by Mitch Barnett, Luke Metcalf and Marata Niukore. They welcome outside backs Will Warbrick and Grant Anderson, with prop Sam McIntyre also joining from the Cowboys. Coach Andrew Webster has done an incredible job with the club, but he has clearly not unlocked the secret to having them perform to their best on the biggest of stages. If anything, their first premiership seems further away after that finish.

North Queensland Cowboys
Last year's ladder finish: 12th

Predicted 2026 finish: 16th

Actual finish: 8th

Grade: C

The fact that the Cowboys somehow snuck into the finals was enough for them to receive a C for their efforts this year. Wildly inconsistent, they could switch on the magic and just about beat anyone, but their defence was appalling at times and ultimately costly. They entered their elimination final needing to tighten up their defence and cut back on their errors, but fell down in both areas. Fullback Scott Drinkwater had a night to both forget and savor in the elimination final against the Sharks, setting up several Cowboys tries while looking completely lost under the high ball.

Overall they got to play in one more game than nine other teams, without ever seriously looking likely to threaten for the title. Their home fans might well remember the season for it's ultimate lowlight: the Round 22 loss to the Roosters which finished in a club record 82-12 flogging.

Where to from here: Scott Drinkwater departs for the Dragons, as the Cowboys go through a minor clean-out. They welcome Joe Chan (Storm), Sione Katoa and Jesse Ramien (both Sharks). Coach Todd Payten will need to spend the entire offseason working on defensive schemes and instilling some commitment to the cause.

Parramatta Eels
Last year's ladder finish: 11th

Predicted 2026 finish: 12th

Actual finish: 13th

Grade: D

The Eels had a frustrating season, often competitive, but rarely consistent. When they were bad, they were very bad, conceding 52 points to the Storm in the opening round, before conceding another 52 to the Titans just five weeks later. They weren't helped by injuries to Mitchell Moses and one-year halves partner Jonah Pezet, but were more often let down by a lack of defensive resolve. Beating the Sharks in Round 26, only to lose to the Dragons in the final round, just about summed up 2026 for the Eels and their long-suffering fans.

Where to from here: They lose a bundle of players for next year, while acquiring Jarome Luai from the Tigers and Jaydn Su'A from the Dragons. It is hard to make any sense of the one-year deal for Luai, even more so with the late-season form of Ronald Volkman, but maybe he will click with Moses and provide more value to the Eels than he did for the Tigers. It is certainly going to be an interesting season for the Eels.

Penrith Panthers
Last year's ladder finish: 7th

Predicted 2026 finish: 1st

Actual finish: 1st (minor premiers)

Grade: B

The Panthers were expected to go very close to winning the premiership this year, after the way they charged home in 2025. They finished the 2026 season atop the ladder and took care of the Roosters first up, before having the week off. Unfortunately, Nathan Cleary broke a bone in his foot against the Roosters and his season was in doubt. He managed to start the preliminary final against the Knights from the bench and entered the game after 25 minutes. Tragically, Cleary was only on the field for 10 minutes before his leg was fractured in a hip drop tackle. From there the Panthers could not manage to overcome the spirited defence of the Knights and bowed out one game short of the big dance for the second year running. What would have been an A-grade season for any other team slips to a B due to the incredibly high standards the Panthers set.

Where to from here: Coach Ivan Cleary enters his last season in charge of the Panthers with no major signings named and just four players; Freddy Lussick, Jack Cole, Scott Sorensen, and Liam Henry leaving. The Panthers talent machine is always churning out future stars, their Jersey Flegg team just smashed the Bulldogs 62-16 in their Grand Final, so no doubt they will once again be the team to beat in 2027.

St George Illawarra Dragons
Last year's ladder finish: 15th

Predicted 2026 finish: 17th

Actual finish: 17th

Grade: D

Nailed it. Pre-season favourites for the wooden spoon, the Dragons lived up to all the hype. A mid-season coach sacking didn't help them as much as it did the Sea Eagles, with Dean Young struggling to squeeze any consistency out of the team. We saw flashes of brilliance from Tyrell Sloane, Jacob Liddle and the Dragons' young forward pack, but nothing short of lethargy at times from players like Valentine Holmes, Moses Suli and Clint Gutherson. When in the right mood, they provided some moments of tough opposition, but doing it week-to-week for a full 80 minutes was beyond them.

Where to from here: Nothing but exciting times ahead for the Dragons as they welcome one of the most bountiful player market raids in the history of rugby league. Scott Drinkwater (Cowboys), Keaon Koloamatangi (Rabbitohs), Luke Metcalf (Warriors), Kodi Nikorima (Dolphins), Phillip Sami (Titans) and Connor Watson (Roosters) will all be joining the Dragons' ever-improving young forwards for what should be a complete transformation. Line up now for those 2027 finals tickets, Dragons fans!

South Sydney Rabbitohs
Last year's finish: 14th

Predicted 2025 finish: 5th

Actual finish: 6th

Grade: C

We expected the Rabbitohs to play finals football and considering the injury issues they suffered through the year, they deserve a C for achieving that goal. It was a little ironic then that their season came to an end largely due to yet another injury, this time to Cody Walker. Walker was the spark that fired up Souths' attack all year, without him they were flat and no match for the energetic Knights. Latrell Mitchell's return at the end of the season was definitely a boost; Cameron Murray was his dominating best around the ruck; and Alex Johnston was busy setting try-scoring records on the wing. There were some questions over whether coach Wayne Bennett was best utilising the talents of Jye Gray through the season, with Matthew Dufty disappointing at times at fullback. It was a disappointing end to what was a very promising season.

Where to from here: Payne Haas arrives from the Broncos next season to joining David Fifita in one of the NRL's most intimidating forward packs. They do lose Keaon Koloamatangi from that pack, but Haas is well established as the best forward in the world. The Rabbitohs will squeeze one more season out of Cody Walker, if they can come to an agreement on how much he is worth. Going on their exit from the finals without him, he is just about priceless.

What a horribly disappointing season for Tigers fans everywhere. The re-built club, with Jarome Luai at the helm, were expected to break their finals drought and started strongly beating the Cowboys, Warriors, Knights and Raiders in the first eight rounds. And then, Luai announced he was signing with the PNG Chiefs for the club's debut 2028 season. The Tigers imploded and it has been a long road of misery since, conceding 52 to the Sharks, 44 to the Storm, 46 to the Sea Eagles, 68 to the Panthers and 56 to the Raiders along the way. They did upset the Roosters in Round 25 to bring a little joy to the black-and-gold army.

Where to from here: Coach Benji Marshall has to somehow wipe 2026 from the players' minds, as he focusses their attention on returning to finals football in 2027. They have made two very astute acquisitions in Jake Averillo (Dolphins) and Jayden Brailey (Raiders). Both are no-nonsense professionals who will sharpen up the Tigers' play and their attitude.
